newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu changes policy, not ideology - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu changes policy, not ideology - analysts.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has done what he said he would never do -- cede part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.
But the Likud party leader's agreement with the PLO to redeploy troops in Hebron is less a strategic shift in ideology than a tactical response to political pressure, analysts say.

"It is very significant that the Likud would sign an agreement to evacuate the city they view as their ancestral hometown," said Khalil al-Shikaki, director of the Centre for Palestine Research and Studies (CPRS).
"But this does not necessarily indicate giving up a long-held ideological stance. It may only reflect political pragmatism on his part," he said.
Gerald Steinberg, a political science professor at Bar Ilan University, said: "It is clearly a pragmatic step. He is responding to the lack of an alternative."
Netanyahu toppled a Labour government last May by opposing the land-for-peace formula underlying the whole five-year-old Middle East peace process.

But the agreement with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to pull troops out of 80 percent of Hebron is the first time a Likud leader has withdrawn from land captured in the 1967 Six-Day War since Menachem Begin left the Sinai Peninsula.

Unlike the Sinai, handed back to Egypt under the 1979 Camp David treaty, Hebron and the rest of the West Bank of the River Jordan are viewed by right-wing Israelis and Jewish settlers as theirs by God-given right.
Analysts say Netanyahu's agreement on Hebron was born more of U.S., Arab and international pressure than of a commitment to the 1993 Palestinian self-rule deal negotiated by Labour in Oslo.
Netanyahu held off implementing Oslo but gunbattles in September which killed 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis prompted Washington to step up pressure in order to salvage its Middle East policy.
Hebron, however, is only Netanyahu's first test. Oslo requires him to withdraw from rural West Bank areas which will eventually shape the borders of an autonomous Palestinian entity.

"He wants to share the West Bank on his terms. And we want him to leave the West Bank in accordance with international resolutions which respect our rights," said Mahdi Abdul-Hadi, director of the Palestinian Academic Society for the Study of International Affairs.
"The two fundamental differences between Likud and Labour are that Labour was committed to a withdrawal process and probably to a Palestinian state," Steinberg said.
"Likud and Netanyahu are not committed to this process but rather each step is measured independently and not seen as part of an overall process," he added.
